newsitem.title: LITHUANIA: VILNIAUS BANK SEEN FACING COMPETITION.
newsitem.headline: VILNIAUS BANK SEEN FACING COMPETITION.

text.p: Lithuania's Vilniaus Bank, which saw its 1996 profits soar, is poised to grab a bigger share of the Baltic state's banking market but will face stiffer competition in 1997, dealers and analysts said on Monday.
The bank announced on Monday that its net profit rose sharply to 24.4 million litas in 1996 from 2.9 million litas the previous year, according to the results of an international audit.
It also said that its share of the Lithuanian banking market doubled in 1996 while its assets increased to 914.7 million litas from 382.9 million litas in the same period.
The bank gave no profit forecasts for 1997.
It is around 90 percent foreign owned is one of the leading blue chip shares on Lithuania's bourse.
"Vilniaus Bank is in a good position to increase its share of the Lithuanian market...the Lithuanian banking market is still relatively small and lacks many services," one local analyst told Reuters.
"For example, its leasing services look like they will expand," he said.
But observers cautioned that the bank, while unquestionably one of the strongest in Lithuania, will face more competition in 1997.
They point out that the bank reaped the benefits of last year's banking crisis, when confidence in many of the country's smaller banks was shaken.
"The bank has certainly benefited from the crisis," one senior western economist said.
"It was viewed as the safest bank in town, and so it got a lot of customers from other banks," he said.
"But other banks, including foreign banks, may enter the market this year and they will compete hard for market share," he added.

In response to the crisis, sparked by the surprise closure of two of the country's top banks in late 1995, the Lithuanian parliament last year lifted restrictions on foreign bank branch operations in the country.
Poland's Kredyt Bank has been given permission to set up shop in Lithuania and Estonian and German banks have expressed interest in following its lead.
Some local banks, such as Hermis Bank, are also expected to give Vilniaus a run for its money this year.
"Other banks will look at what Vilniaus Bank has done and will try to do the same," Tomas Adrejauskas, a dealer with brokerage firm Suprema, told Reuters.
"Vilniaus should increase its market share this year, but not as substantially as it did last year," he said.
